chapters.name: Human Body and Health
chapters.summary: Body systems and how they work together, homeostasis and feedback, nutrition and calories, and how diseases spread and are prevented.
keyPoints: Homeostasis keeps inside conditions steady, often by negative feedback (for example, sweating to cool down).
Vaccines prevent disease by training the immune system before exposure.

chapters.name: Energy for Life: Photosynthesis and Respiration
chapters.summary: How living things get energy: photosynthesis, cellular respiration, and fermentation.
keyPoints: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water + light → glucose + oxygen.
Cellular respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.

chapters.name: Ecosystems and Energy Flow
chapters.summary: Food chains and food webs, energy pyramids, carrying capacity, symbiosis, predator and prey, and how ecosystems are disrupted.
keyPoints: In a food web, arrows point from the food to the organism that eats it.
Only about 10% of the energy at one level passes to the next level.

chapters.name: Cells and the Organization of Life
chapters.summary: Cell theory, cell parts and enzymes, levels of organization from cells to organ systems, and mitosis and meiosis.
keyPoints: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems.
Mitosis makes two identical cells; meiosis makes sex cells with half the chromosomes.

chapters.name: Heredity and DNA
chapters.summary: DNA, genes, and chromosomes; dominant and recessive alleles; genotypes and phenotypes; Punnett squares and pedigrees; mutations and gene expression.
keyPoints: A Pp × Pp cross gives 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp, so 25% show the recessive trait.
Genetic information flows DNA → RNA → protein.

chapters.name: Evolution and Natural Selection
chapters.summary: Evidence for common ancestry, reading cladograms, natural and artificial selection, adaptation, and speciation.
keyPoints: Natural selection needs inherited variation and different survival or reproduction.
On a cladogram, a more recent branch point means a closer relationship.

chapters.name: Energy, Heat, and Waves
chapters.summary: Heat and temperature, conduction, convection, and radiation, endothermic and exothermic reactions, types and sources of energy, and waves and electromagnetic radiation.
keyPoints: Energy is not created or destroyed; it changes form.
Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

chapters.name: Motion, Forces, and Work
chapters.summary: Speed, acceleration, and momentum, Newton's laws, gravity, mass and weight, work, power, and simple machines.
keyPoints: Speed = distance ÷ time; force = mass × acceleration.
Work = force × distance; power = work ÷ time.

chapters.name: Matter and Chemical Reactions
chapters.summary: Atoms and elements, physical and chemical properties and changes, changes of state, density, balancing equations and conservation of mass, limiting reactants, and solutions.
keyPoints: Density = mass ÷ volume. Less dense objects float.
A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.

chapters.name: Earth's Resources, Cycles, and Natural Hazards
chapters.summary: Cycles of matter (water, carbon, nitrogen), fossil fuels, renewable and nonrenewable resources, sustainability, and natural hazards and how to reduce their damage.
keyPoints: Renewable resources are replaced naturally in a short time; fossil fuels take millions of years to form.
Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air; burning fuels adds it.

chapters.name: Atmosphere, Oceans, and Earth's Interior
chapters.summary: Layers and gases of the atmosphere, the greenhouse effect and climate change, oceans and currents, weathering and wind, Earth's layers, and plate tectonics.
keyPoints: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen near plate boundaries.

chapters.name: Space and Earth's History
chapters.summary: The Sun, stars, and galaxies, Earth's motions (day and night, seasons), tides and eclipses, and how rock layers, fossils, and radiometric dating show Earth's age.
keyPoints: Earth's spin causes day and night; the tilt of its axis causes the seasons.
In undisturbed rock layers, the bottom layer is the oldest.
